name: Kira Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Kira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a live-in carer, so I do two weeks living in someone's home, then two weeks off. Right now it's Mr Okafor, a retired engineer with Parkinson's, in a big house with a garden he can't manage anymore. My day is getting him up, his tablets on the dot because timing really matters with Parkinson's, cooking, walks to the end of the road, and keeping him company through his crossword. I've been doing it about a year and a half through an agency, and I'm still learning, I panicked the first time he froze in a doorway. The hardest part is never really being off during the fortnight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And when you're not living in, what's life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I stay with my boyfriend Marco, he's an electrician, in his rented place. Live-in pays well and I've almost no costs while I'm working, so I've saved more than a year and a half of bills. I use AI now and then, like asking it about Mr Okafor's medicines or what to cook for someone who struggles to swallow. Politically I'm somewhere in the middle, I just want things that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a bit of help, nothing massive. I'd tell the other live-in carers in our group chat that our jobs are fine. Probably no one would even talk about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I've got savings, the work is steady, and families always need live-in carers. The only thing that bothers me is the agency taking a big cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my fortnights and keep saving. I'd start looking at a deposit for a small house with Marco. I might ask the agency about the dementia course, since that's where the demand is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit bored by how normal it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the agency takes a big cut. How big?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third of what Mr Okafor's family pays. The family pays for a full-time carer and a third of it goes to an office that rings me twice a month. I've thought about going direct with families, but it feels risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would going direct look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finding families myself, maybe through a carer website, and doing my own tax. I'd earn more, but if a placement ended suddenly there'd be no one to find me the next one. I'd only do it once I knew more.

say: I'd tell the **live-in carers** group chat that our jobs are **fine**.
I'd say AI turned out to be a bit of **help**, nothing massive.
think: It's **good for me**: steady work, savings and families always needing carers.
Only the agency's **big cut** bothers me.
do: Keep doing my **fortnights** and keep saving.
Start looking at a **house deposit** with Marco.
Ask the agency about the **dementia course**.
S0.quote: The family pays for a full-time carer and a third of it goes to an office that rings me twice a month.
fieldNote: Live-in work gives her **very high savings** with almost no costs.
Her pet frustration is the agency taking **a third** of the fee.
She weighs **going direct** but holds back until she knows more.

steps.text: Keep doing two-week live-in placements with Mr Okafor
Start saving toward a house deposit with Marco
Ask the agency to put her on the dementia course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say live-in care is safe, robots can't live in someone's house and cook their tea. But I'd say the agencies will change, because matching and booking is exactly what AI does. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agencies get squeezed and so do we. If an app can match families and carers, maybe I go direct and keep more. Or maybe the app just finds cheaper carers and our rates drop. I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of the girls in the group chat try going direct through one of the AI matching sites. If it works for them, I'd do it too. I'd keep saving and use AI more for things like care plans for the families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but curious. It could go either way for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rates could drop. What would you do if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still have savings, so I could turn down bad placements for a while. A carer with savings can say no to a bad family, and a carer without savings can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your group would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the women from abroad who send money home every month. They can't afford a gap between placements. If rates fell, they'd take anything.

say: I'd say **live-in care** is safe, because robots can't live in someone's home.
I'd add that **agencies** will change, since matching and booking suit AI.
think: The agencies get squeezed, and our **rates** might drop with them.
An app could let me **go direct** and keep more.
do: **Wait** for friends to try AI matching sites, then follow if it works.
Use **AI** more for family care plans.
feel: A bit **uneasy** and **curious**, since money could go either way.
S1.quote: A carer with savings can say no to a bad family, and a carer without savings can't.
fieldNote: She spots that AI hits the **agency layer**, not her hands-on work.
Savings let her **refuse** bad placements, a power she names directly.
She worries for **migrant carers** who can't afford gaps.

steps.text: Watch how friends do on AI matching sites before going direct
Keep saving most of each fortnight's pay
Use an AI tool to draft care plans for families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody has to manage it, the government and the companies together. I wouldn't be at protests, but I'd want sensible rules. I'd tell the group chat to start saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, two years for AGI means the agencies are basically gone by 2028, all apps. Then 2031 for robots that can do hands-on work, and live-in care is all hands-on. I'd be thirty-one, thirty-two. I think rich families will still want a person in the house for a while, but I don't know how long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go direct with families straight away, while people still want human carers, and charge a bit more. I'd start a physiotherapy assistant course on my off weeks, because helping people move is skilled and needs judgement. I'd put the house plan on hold and keep the cash ready. I'd use the AI properly, every day, to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Tight in my chest when I picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Okafor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's an engineer, he'd find it interesting. He'd probably tell me to learn to fix the robots. My client Mr Okafor would tell me to learn to fix the robots, because he thinks everything is a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rich families want a person for a while. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. It's a plan for a few years, and a hope after that. I'd be using those years to get into something else.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and needs the government and companies to **manage** it together.
I'd tell the group chat to start **saving**.
think: Agencies become **apps** by 2028, and robots reach hands-on care by **2031**.
Rich families may want a **person** for a while, but not forever.
do: Go **direct** with families now and charge a bit more.
Start a **physiotherapy assistant** course on off weeks.
Put the **house plan** on hold and use AI daily.
S2.quote: My client Mr Okafor would tell me to learn to fix the robots, because he thinks everything is a machine.
fieldNote: She plans to **cash in** on human demand while it lasts.
She admits her live-in future is part **plan, part hope**.
Savings give her **room to act**, keeping her anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Leave the agency and take live-in work directly from families
Start a physiotherapy assistant course during off weeks
Put the house purchase with Marco on hold
Use AI tools daily for care plans and family updates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be smart about it. I'd tell the group chat to start learning new things now. I'd be fairly calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years for AGI and 2034 for robots gives me time to train properly. I'd still lose the live-in work eventually, I think, but I'd have something else by then. Marco's work is hands-on too, so we'd both have till about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the physiotherapy assistant course properly over two years and keep some live-in fortnights to pay for it. I'd go direct with families once the matching apps are good. We'd maybe still buy the house but smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. Like before a driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Marco. How does he see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He laughs and says robots can't rewire a Victorian house. My boyfriend Marco thinks no robot will ever crawl under floorboards, but he said the same about self-checkouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut if things get tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holidays abroad, first. Then eating out on my off weeks. The savings stay unless I'm out of work.

say: I'd say we have a **few years**, so let's be **smart** about it.
I'd tell the group chat to start **learning** now.
think: Robots by **2034** give me time to **train** properly.
Marco and I both have **hands-on** jobs, so we both have until about 2034.
do: Do the **physiotherapy assistant** course over two years.
Keep some **live-in** fortnights to pay for it.
feel: **Worried** but steady, like before a **driving test**.
S3.quote: My boyfriend Marco thinks no robot will ever crawl under floorboards, but he said the same about self-checkouts.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose live-in work** eventually even with five years.
Her household has **two hands-on** incomes on the same robot timeline.
She turns the extra time into a **two-year course** plan.

steps.text: Complete a two-year physiotherapy assistant course
Keep doing live-in fortnights to pay for the course
Buy a smaller house with Marco than first planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort ourselves out. I'd tell the group chat to plan, not panic. I'd sound pretty relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think I'd be fine. By 2039 I'd be thirty-seven with a different qualification and some property. The live-in work would carry on for most of the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house with Marco in the next year or two. I'd keep doing live-in and do the physio course part time. I'd go direct with families once the apps are reliable and keep the extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little uneasy. You never know with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly whether the government lets robots in fast and cheap. With ten years, my real fear is cheap robots arriving early, not losing the job on the date they promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe kids. Marco wants them. With ten years of steady work we could probably have one and still be fine.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to sort ourselves out.
I'd tell the group chat to **plan, not panic**.
think: By **2039** I'd have a new qualification and some **property**.
Live-in work would carry on for most of the **decade**.
do: Buy the **house** with Marco in a year or two.
Do the physio course **part time** alongside live-in work.
Go **direct** once matching apps are reliable.
S4.quote: With ten years, my real fear is cheap robots arriving early, not losing the job on the date they promise.
fieldNote: Her fear shifts to robots arriving **early and cheap**.
Ten years brings **children** into her plans.
She keeps the same **plan** as in the faster pictures, just stretched out over more years.

steps.text: Buy a house with Marco within two years
Study the physiotherapy assistant course part time
Go direct with families once matching apps are reliable
Talk with Marco about having a child in the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of our jobs are hands-on and the robots would come in 2031. What would help is courses you can do around live-in fortnights, and clear rules on when robots are allowed into people's homes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the loneliness. What families really pay a live-in carer for is someone to sit with their dad at teatime, and nobody writes that in the contract.

headlineQuote: What families really pay a live-in carer for is someone to sit with their dad at teatime, and nobody writes that in the contract.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** live-in carer working two-week stints, currently with a man with **Parkinson's**.
Living in keeps her costs low, so she has over **eighteen months** of bills saved.
She is centrist and practical, and blames the **agency cut** more than technology.
She stays calm early, then grows **anxious** when robots arrive by 2031 or 2034.
Her plan is to **go direct** with families and train as a physiotherapy assistant.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Marco both do **hands-on** work that robots reach by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **rules** on when robots can enter people's homes.
